doc.title: Dick Spottswood interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 13, 2023

title: False attributions and well-meaning discography
summary: He criticizes guesswork in discography, citing the Clay Custer / George W. Thomas rumor, and admits he has been wrong in his own writing.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well a lot of jazz discography consists of well-meaning guesswork I think. But I don’t think we’re any better off for it. Because sometimes if you have information like that that you think is accurate then it’s going to discourage you from trying to look for what might actually be the case. You know that famous recording — not famous — famous to record collectors, of George W. Thomas’s “The Rocks” by a young pianist represented as Clay Custer, a 1923 recording? Do you know that record? Well it’s represented as being George W. Thomas and it sounds like a high school kid who could barely read the sheet music trying to play the record and that’s the performance. I guess that there are a couple of surviving records but Thomas himself, the acknowledged pianist — and those records are good, “The Rocks” the guy playing “The Rocks” were good. But the record collectors swear to God that it’s Clay Custer and George W. Thomas are one and the same person. And once those rumors get started sometimes they’re kind of what Tintin Books called it “the lies that will not die.” You know? There are a lot of false attributions like Norris Turney I think.
Oh yes, and like the way Bessie Smith passed away and so forth.
Yeah. Very well meaning and understandable in the context of the time but in the long run they’re not doing history much of a service.
Would you ever go back and edit anything you’ve written and then found out through your own research, ensuing research, that I would amend that?

Sure. Don’t ask me for — I’d have to think about what they were but I’ve said things that I’ve been wrong about because they seemed accurate at the time. But I can’t remember what they were. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
